definition: PingOne's own MCP endpoint, run by Ping, for the Management API admin plane. This app connects to it as a client, lists its tools and calls them. Endpoint shape: https://api.pingone.{region}/v1/environments/{envId}/mcp (pingone-mcp skill; a second shape seen in AI-DEMO2 is UNVERIFIED).
The part of PingOne that manages PingOne itself: applications, populations, users, DaVinci flows, environment configuration. It is not your own product's data or end-user tools.

A PingOne application with admin roles, used by unattended callers such as scripts and services. Give it only the roles the caller needs: an overprivileged worker is as risky as an overprivileged REST credential.

The OAuth grant a worker application uses: it presents its own client id and secret at the token endpoint and gets a bearer token. The secret is only ever sent to the token endpoint; the MCP endpoint gets the bearer token.

The interactive sign-in: the admin is sent to the authorization server, approves, and comes back with a code that is exchanged using a one-time secret (the PKCE verifier, S256). This app adds state and nonce, checks the issuer, and accepts the callback only on the exact registered loopback redirect URI.

The server lists only the tools the calling identity's admin roles allow. A short list usually means missing roles, not a broken server (pingone-mcp skill). The same URL shows different tools to a viewer and an admin.

Prefer the hosted MCP tools for application, population and user reads, user management and DaVinci reads; fall back to the Management API for what MCP does not cover, and on any MCP failure do not retry in a loop (pingone-mcp skill).
Every tool is classed read, write or destructive. Write and destructive calls are blocked until the operator turns on allow writes for that connection. Unknown tools count as write.

Even with writes allowed, a write call is refused until the request carries confirm:true and the hash of the exact arguments that were shown. Destructive calls also need the tool name typed. Change one argument and the hash no longer matches.

A local, append-only record of every call, allowed or blocked: when, which connection, which tool, its class, the outcome, the arguments (secret-looking keys redacted) and their hash. Secrets and tokens are scrubbed before anything is written.
